\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

All tables and figures in this section report values computed from the experimental runs.

\subsection{RQ1: Reasoning}
\label{sec:rq1}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\input{figures/fig_rq1_panels.pgf}
\caption{The change from reasoning off to on, per model and dataset; each bar is one model on one
dataset. (a) Agreement change (QWK on minus off); above zero, reasoning improved agreement with the
teacher grades. (b) Change in run-to-run consistency (within-item SD, off minus on); below zero,
reasoning made the grader less consistent. (c) How many times more output tokens reasoning used, on a
log scale because the ratios range from about 10 to over 900. Table~\ref{tab:rq1values} lists the
values.}
\label{fig:rq1}
\end{figure*}

\input{tables/tab_rq1_values}

Reasoning is compared on the sampled items graded both with reasoning off and with reasoning on,
keeping the items whose reasoning stayed within the output-token limit (Section~\ref{sec:metrics}).
Fig.~\ref{fig:rq1} shows, for each model on each dataset, what turning reasoning on changed: (a)
agreement with the teacher grades, (b) run-to-run consistency, and (c) the number of output tokens.
Table~\ref{tab:rq1values} gives the values.

Reasoning raised agreement significantly in five of the twenty combinations, four of them for Qwen3.5.
It helped Qwen3.5 on four of its five datasets: by 0.071 QWK on Mohler (from a reasoning-off level of 0.622), 0.098 on SemEval (from
0.533), 0.250 on RIAYN (from 0.561), and 0.113 on PT-CS code (from 0.493). Its PT-CS short-answer gain
(0.092) is not significant. The only other significant gain is GPT-5.1 on RIAYN, by 0.228 (from 0.561).
These five gains are judged one comparison at a time; after Holm's correction for the twenty
comparisons (Section~\ref{sec:metrics}), only the two RIAYN gains, for Qwen3.5 and GPT-5.1, remain
significant. Everywhere else no gain was detected. For two of those cases the data go further: on
Mohler, the gains for GLM-5.1 ($+0.005$) and GPT-5.1 ($+0.006$) are equivalent to zero, meaning their
90\% intervals lie inside the margin of $\pm0.05$ QWK fixed in advance. The other intervals are too wide
to call the two settings equivalent, especially on PT-CS, where the comparisons rest on 25 to 67 items.

The gains came at a price with two parts. First, tokens: reasoning multiplied output tokens by 9 to 925
times, and the premium depends on the domain. For GLM-5.1, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and GPT-5.1, reasoning used
9 to 62 times as many output tokens on short answers and 109 to 211 times on code; Qwen3.5, whose
reasoning runs longest, used 666 to 925 times as many on both (Fig.~\ref{fig:rq1}c). Second, consistency: the within-item SD across
repetitions rose from off to on in 17 of the 20 combinations (in two of them by less than 0.001) and fell
in three, GLM-5.1 on PT-CS code and GPT-5.1 on PT-CS short answers and on RIAYN (Fig.~\ref{fig:rq1}b).
Grades varied across repetitions even at temperature 0: with reasoning off, 9 to 60\% of items received
different grades across repetitions, depending on the model and dataset. Reasoning therefore cost
reproducibility whether or not it improved agreement. Part of this loss follows from length, since items
with longer outputs varied more, but only in part: the rank correlation between an item's output length
and the spread of its grades was moderate (median 0.46 over the model-dataset combinations) and uneven,
from 0.08 for GPT-5.1 on Mohler to 0.76 for GLM-5.1 on RIAYN. Consistency is also no guarantee of
quality: with reasoning off, Qwen3.5 was the most reproducible grader on four of the five datasets (SD
0.011 to 0.021), including PT-CS code, where it graded worst.

One code-specific failure shapes how the code results must be read. On PT-CS code, Qwen3.5 with
reasoning off scores 49\% of the answers as exactly zero, against 2\% for the teachers. We call this behaviour the \emph{zero-collapse}: answers that deserve partial credit
receive the same score as an empty answer, so the grader can no longer tell weak answers apart. A grader
that instead spreads its scores across the scale, as the teachers do, we call \emph{discriminating}. The
zeros are genuine, parseable scores, and they recur whether the exam is graded whole or one question at
a time. On the 67 items graded both ways, reasoning roughly halved Qwen3.5's zeros (from 47\% to 24\%), and
its $+0.113$ gain came with that drop. GPT-5.1 shows a milder form of the same behaviour: with reasoning off it scores 32\% of
the PT-CS code answers and 17\% of RIAYN's as zero, against 2\% and 5\% for the teachers, and Qwen3.5
does the same on RIAYN (16\%). With reasoning off, these two models were also the two weakest code graders on the answers all four
models graded: 0.544 and 0.561 on RIAYN and 0.468 and 0.584 on PT-CS code, against 0.61 to 0.73 for the
other two. The significant code gains all belong to them, although GPT-5.1's gain on
PT-CS code ($+0.061$) is not significant. GLM-5.1 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, which score 9
to 13\% of the code answers as zero, gained little from reasoning on either code dataset. The
configuration guide (Section~\ref{sec:framework}) therefore keys its code advice to whether a model
collapses rather than to the model's name.

Overall, reasoning raised agreement significantly in five of twenty combinations, two after Holm's
correction, multiplied output tokens by 9 to 925, and lowered consistency in seventeen. On short answers
every public gain was positive but at most 0.10 QWK, and none survived the correction. On code the gains
were the largest in the study, 0.11 to 0.25, but only for the two models that scored too many answers as
zero; for GLM-5.1 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash agreement moved by $-0.048$ to $+0.076$ at 109 to 192 times the
tokens. Reasoning helps a collapsing code grader and adds little to a sound one.

\subsection{RQ2: Evaluation Guidance}
\label{sec:rq2}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\input{figures/fig_rq2_guidance.pgf}
\caption{Change in agreement ($\Delta$QWK, K=5, with 95\% confidence intervals) when evaluation guidance,
the reference answer or rubric, is added to the question and student answer, per dataset and model.
Reasoning off.}
\label{fig:rq2}
\end{figure}

Evaluation guidance adds the reference answer or the rubric to the question and student answer: a
reference answer on Mohler and SemEval, and a rubric on RIAYN and on both parts of PT-CS. We measured it
on three model families, Qwen3.5, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and GPT-5.1, each with reasoning off, on all five
sets (Fig.~\ref{fig:rq2}).

Guidance raised agreement significantly in 13 of the 15 model-dataset combinations, and all thirteen
gains remain significant after Holm's correction. Without guidance the models agreed with the teachers
at 0.32 to 0.57 QWK; the significant gains run from 0.095 (DeepSeek-V4-Flash on Mohler, from 0.523) to
0.335 (Qwen3.5 on PT-CS short answers, from 0.317). They are as large on the deployment data as on the
public data: on the 295 PT-CS code answers the rubric adds 0.146 for Qwen3.5, 0.148 for
DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and 0.190 for GPT-5.1. Of the two exceptions, DeepSeek-V4-Flash on PT-CS short
answers gained 0.112 without reaching significance on 84 items, and GPT-5.1 on RIAYN was unchanged
($-0.005$, CI $[-0.13,+0.12]$). Guidance did not make grading more consistent: the within-item SD rose
in 10 of the 15 combinations, by at most 0.028 of the scale.

Overall, evaluation guidance is the most reliable gain in the study: it raised agreement by 0.10 to 0.34
QWK in 13 of 15 combinations, all surviving Holm's correction, across three model families and both
domains. It cost 1.2 to 1.8 times as much per grade as grading without it, for the longer prompt, and left
consistency almost unchanged. The practical reading is simple: add a trustworthy rubric or reference
answer whenever one exists.

\subsection{RQ3: Scope and Decomposition}
\label{sec:rq3}

A grade can be requested in more than one shape. Scope is whether the whole exam is graded in one call
or one question at a time; decomposition is whether each answer gets a single holistic score or is
scored criterion by criterion. In the decomposition contrast the model sees the same rubric either way;
criterion-by-criterion scoring only asks it to score each criterion separately and sum the scores. We
compare each shape against the baseline, one question per call with a single holistic score, on two
model families, Qwen3.5 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, with reasoning off (Fig.~\ref{fig:rq3}). Scope needs
complete exams, so it is measured on PT-CS code; decomposition is measured on PT-CS code and on RIAYN,
whose rubrics mark each step of one or more accepted solution paths. Both contrasts are scored against
each answer's final grade.

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\input{figures/fig_rq3_scope_decomp.pgf}
\caption{Scope and decomposition contrasts ($\Delta$QWK, K=5, with 95\% confidence intervals), per model:
grading the whole exam in one call instead of question by question (PT-CS code), and scoring criterion
by criterion instead of holistically (RIAYN and PT-CS code). Below zero means the alternative scored worse
than the baseline. Dashed lines mark the $\pm0.05$ equivalence margin. Reasoning off.}
\label{fig:rq3}
\end{figure}

Across the 295 PT-CS code questions, grading the whole exam in one call lowered agreement for Qwen3.5 by
0.091 QWK (CI $[-0.13,-0.05]$), from 0.468 with one question per call, and the loss remains significant
after Holm's correction. For DeepSeek-V4-Flash the change was $-0.024$ (CI $[-0.07,+0.03]$), not
significant. Scoring criterion by criterion brought no significant gain either: the four changes run
from $-0.072$ (DeepSeek-V4-Flash on PT-CS code, significant after correction) to $+0.029$ (Qwen3.5 on
RIAYN, not significant). None of the six intervals fits inside the $\pm0.05$ margin, so the data do not
show the shapes to be equivalent; they show that no alternative did significantly better, and that two
did significantly worse.

Cost does not favour the alternatives either. Per question, grading the whole exam in one call cost
Qwen3.5 7\% more than one call per question, because the joint answer carries more output tokens, and
saved DeepSeek-V4-Flash only 6\%; scoring criterion by criterion cost 1.3 to 3.1 times as much per answer as a single holistic score,
because the per-criterion breakdown lengthens the output.

Overall, of the six contrasts against the baseline shape none improved agreement and two lowered it
significantly (the whole exam by 0.091 for Qwen3.5, criterion scoring by 0.072 for DeepSeek-V4-Flash),
while the whole exam changed the cost per question by $-6$ to $+7$\% and criterion scoring multiplied it
by 1.3 to 3.1. Question-by-question, holistic grading is therefore the default.

\subsection{RQ4: Models and Cost}
\label{sec:cost}

The four model families differ both in how well they grade and in what they cost. We compare eight
configurations, the four models each with reasoning off and on, all with guidance and one question per
call. Fig.~\ref{fig:perdataset} gives agreement per dataset, and Fig.~\ref{fig:costquality} weighs it
against cost on the public datasets, grouped into the two tasks, short answers (Mohler and SemEval) and
code (RIAYN). Both figures score every configuration on the same items, those that all eight graded
(the reasoning samples), so that no configuration is favoured by an easier set of items. On the public
datasets the eight configurations reach a mean QWK of 0.556 to 0.667 across the three datasets, and the
per-dataset winner changes: on Mohler it is Qwen3.5 with reasoning on (0.659), on SemEval GLM-5.1 with
reasoning on (0.590), and on RIAYN GLM-5.1 with reasoning on (0.803).

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\input{figures/fig3_per_dataset_config.pgf}
\caption{Agreement (QWK, K=5, item means, bootstrap CIs) by model and reasoning mode, per dataset,
with guidance and one question per call, on the items that all eight configurations graded: 175 on
Mohler and SemEval, 149 on RIAYN, and 99 on PT-CS (67 code and 32 short answers, pooled).}
\label{fig:perdataset}
\end{figure}

These absolute levels are best read against the agreement between humans. Mohler gives two teachers'
grades for every answer, and the two agree with each other at QWK 0.49 over its 2273 answers. On the
same answers, the four models with reasoning off agree with the teachers' mean at 0.62 to 0.64, with the
first teacher at 0.73 to 0.75, and with the second at 0.39 to 0.41. The models' agreement with each
teacher brackets the teachers' agreement with each other, so the remaining disagreement between model and
teacher on Mohler is of the size that separates two human graders.

As a complement to QWK, which treats SemEval's binary label as the two ends of the scale, we report
accuracy and AUROC. Over the 800 SemEval items and their repetitions, with reasoning off, the models label
answers correctly 0.76 to 0.79 of the time, with AUROC 0.83 to 0.85, so they separate correct from
incorrect answers well above chance. The fixed 0.5 cutoff does not flatter these figures: for every model
it is within 0.024 accuracy of the best cutoff between 0.30 and 0.70.

The configuration mattered far more on code than on short answers. On short answers the eight
configurations fall within 0.074 QWK of each other, but on code they span 0.259, three and a half times
as much (Fig.~\ref{fig:costquality}a and~b).

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\input{figures/fig_rq4_cost.pgf}
\caption{Agreement versus cost on the public datasets, one point per model and reasoning mode:
(a) short answers (mean QWK over Mohler and SemEval), (b) code (RIAYN). Agreement is computed on the items
all eight configurations graded. The horizontal axis is the cost of 1000 grades in euros, on a log scale
because costs span more than three orders of magnitude. Points up and to the left are better. Cost is
computed from the logged tokens at the providers' billed per-token rates.}
\label{fig:costquality}
\end{figure}

Cost separates the configurations far more than agreement does. On short answers cost spans more than two
orders of magnitude (\euro{}0.02 to \euro{}6.3 per thousand grades) while agreement moves by at most
0.074: in Fig.~\ref{fig:costquality}a, the four models with reasoning off (circles) reach 0.550 to 0.585
at \euro{}0.02 to \euro{}0.34, and turning reasoning on adds 0.014 to 0.062, at 3 to 200 times the cost.
The largest of these gains, Qwen3.5's, is the one that is significant in Section~\ref{sec:rq1}. Among the
models with reasoning off, GLM-5.1 agrees best (0.585 at \euro{}0.20). On code
(Fig.~\ref{fig:costquality}b), reasoning lifted agreement for every family, significantly for two of the
four (Section~\ref{sec:rq1}). GLM-5.1 leads at 0.726 with reasoning off (\euro{}0.95) and 0.803 with
reasoning on (\euro{}6.4). For Qwen3.5 the code gain (0.544 to 0.754) came with fewer zeros (16\% to 9\%
of the answers). On the public data the closed frontier model is never the efficient choice: with
reasoning off GPT-5.1 agrees less than GLM-5.1 on both tasks at a higher cost, and on code its best result
with reasoning (0.791, \euro{}30 per thousand grades) sits below GLM-5.1 with reasoning (0.803,
\euro{}6.4) and only 0.065 above GLM-5.1 without it, at 31 times the cost.

Cost also carries an operational lesson. All the experiments together (whole-exam cost counted once per
call) cost \euro{}103.9 at the providers' billed rates: \euro{}50.4 on OpenAI and \euro{}53.4 on
DeepInfra. Before the runs, we estimated the cost of the comparisons planned at the outset by pricing
every planned call at list price, using typical input and output lengths from pilot runs; that estimate
was \euro{}16.7, while those comparisons cost \euro{}61.0, 3.7 times more. On OpenAI, where the budgeted
price was right, the estimate was 1.9 times too low only because reasoning traces ran longer than the
pilots; the first reasoning runs even had to be repeated with the output limit raised eightfold (4096 to
32\,768 tokens). On DeepInfra it was 4.5 times too low, because the prices we budgeted were also below
those the provider billed. Practitioners budgeting a reasoning-on grading arm should price it at the
provider's current billed rates and expect output several times longer than a pilot suggests.

Overall, GLM-5.1 is the efficient all-rounder: with reasoning off it is the best grader of the four on both
tasks (0.585 on short answers, 0.726 on code), at under one euro per thousand grades. Reasoning raised
agreement on both tasks, but on short answers by at most 0.062 at up to 200 times the cost, and on code
significantly only for the two models that gave too many zeros (Section~\ref{sec:rq1}). Reasoning off is
therefore the dependable default, with reasoning on reserved for models that collapse or for budgets that
put agreement first. The configuration guide (Section~\ref{sec:framework}) builds this rule in and tests its
default against the best configuration on each dataset.

\subsection{RQ5: Conversation State}
\label{sec:rq5}

Grades can be shaped not only by how each answer is scored, but by how the whole grading session is
run. This sub-study varies whether each of a student's answers is graded in its own clean conversation
or inside one shared conversation that accumulates across that student's exam. Within the shared
conversation it also varies the order in which the answers are presented: the exam's own question
order, or the reverse. It needs complete multi-question exams, which only the deployment provides.
Qwen3.5 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash graded 80 complete code exams five times each; GLM-5.1 graded the first 20
of the same exams three times. Everything else is held at the baseline configuration.

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\input{figures/fig5_conversation.pgf}
\caption{Conversation sub-study, per model, with 95\% confidence intervals: (a) mean grade in one shared,
accumulating conversation minus the mean grade with a clean conversation per answer; (b) answer order
within the shared conversation, as the mean absolute change per answer between the exam's own order and
the reverse (solid) and the mean signed change (hatched). Grades as a fraction of the scale. Qwen3.5 and
DeepSeek-V4-Flash: 80 code exams, $k=5$; GLM-5.1: the first 20 of those exams, $k=3$.}
\label{fig:conversation}
\end{figure}

Grading inside one shared, accumulating conversation lowered grades for every model
(Fig.~\ref{fig:conversation}a), but only slightly: by 0.012 of the scale for Qwen3.5 (Wilcoxon
$p=.03$), 0.010 for DeepSeek-V4-Flash ($p=.18$, not significant), and 0.027 for GLM-5.1 ($p=.003$).
Answer order mattered more for individual grades (Fig.~\ref{fig:conversation}b): the same answer scored
differently depending on its position, by 8\% of the question's marks on average for Qwen3.5 and
DeepSeek-V4-Flash and 10\% for GLM-5.1. On the 80 exams the order also shifted the average grade a
little, but in opposite directions for the two models: the exam's own order scored 0.013 higher for
DeepSeek-V4-Flash ($p<.001$) and 0.015 lower for Qwen3.5 ($p=.004$), while GLM-5.1 showed no shift on
its 20 exams. Position therefore adds variation with no general direction. Because Qwen3.5's
zero-collapse can hide order effects (an answer scored zero cannot move down), the other two models are
the cleaner read.

Overall, how the session is run matters, more for individual grades than for averages. A shared history
pulled grades slightly down, and answer order moved individual grades by 8 to 10\% of the question's
marks, in a direction that depended on the model. Grading each answer in a clean conversation avoids both, which
recommends it on fairness grounds: a student's grade should not depend on where an answer fell in the
session.

\subsection{RQ6: Transfer to the Deployment Context}
\label{sec:rq6}

\begin{figure}[!b]
\centering
\input{figures/fig_rq6_transfer.pgf}
\caption{Transfer of the configuration ranking from the public datasets to the deployment context,
within each domain: (a) public short answers (mean over Mohler and SemEval) against PT-CS short
answers, (b) public code (RIAYN) against PT-CS code. Each line is one configuration (a model
with reasoning on or off); the vertical axis is agreement with the human grade (QWK, K=5), on the items
that all eight configurations graded: 175 on Mohler and SemEval, 149 on RIAYN, 32 PT-CS short answers,
and 67 PT-CS code answers.}
\label{fig:transfer}
\end{figure}

The last comparison asks whether the ranking of configurations found on the public datasets carries over
to a real deployment context. PT-CS, with its 379 teacher-validated answers from a live grading platform,
is that context. PT-CS has already appeared in the earlier questions, one factor at a time: guidance raised
agreement on PT-CS code by 0.146 to 0.190, inside the public range (Section~\ref{sec:rq2}), and the
zero-collapse appeared on PT-CS code as on RIAYN (Section~\ref{sec:rq1}). The question here concerns the
whole ranking: does the configuration that ranks best on the public datasets also rank best in
deployment? The public ranking is computed from the public datasets alone, and the comparison is made
within domain, public short answers against PT-CS short answers and public code against PT-CS code, with
every configuration scored on the same items.

The ranking carried over only loosely (Fig.~\ref{fig:transfer}). On code the public and deployment
orderings agree in direction, Spearman $\rho=0.64$ (where 1 would be an identical order and 0 an unrelated
one), but with eight configurations this is not significant ($p=.09$). The ends hold: GLM-5.1 is first on
both sides (with reasoning on for the public data, 0.803, and off for PT-CS, 0.676), and Qwen3.5 with
reasoning off, held down by its zero-collapse, is last on both. On short answers the order did not carry
over ($\rho=0.21$, $p=.61$): the public configurations are separated by only 0.074 QWK, and the 32 PT-CS
short answers reorder them, with GPT-5.1 with reasoning off first on PT-CS (0.826) and sixth on the public
data. Absolute levels also shift between contexts, up on PT-CS short answers and mostly down on PT-CS
code.

Overall, what transferred to the deployment were the effects and the failure mode, not the fine ranking.
Guidance helped as much on PT-CS as on the public data, the collapsing model graded code worst in both
settings, and GLM-5.1 led code grading in both; the order of configurations that differ by a few hundredths
of QWK did not carry over. A configuration chosen on public data is therefore a sound start, and the choice
between close configurations should be confirmed on local, teacher-graded answers, which is the check the
guide builds in.
